summary: Gathers what is needed to introduce domain-style names across the DDN/MILNET Internet community. It gives an overview of moving from host tables to domains, a timetable for the move, and references to related documents and software, as an aid for implementors and administrators.

plainLanguage.summary: Before domain names, a machine that wanted to reach another machine had to look the address up in a list of every host on the network. This RFC is the plan for replacing that list with the hierarchical system of names and name servers, and it lays out how the changeover was to happen and by when. It is also a signpost to the documents describing the system and to the software that implemented it.

questions: how did milnet move to domain names
what was the transition from host tables to dns
when was the host table discontinued
what is the difference between a host table and the domain system
subtitle: The 1987 plan for moving the MILNET community from host tables to domain names.

tldr.problem: MILNET machines found each other's addresses by looking up a single table of every host in the network, copied from a central registry. The table had grown to the point where it could no longer be managed, and every host on the network would be affected by the move to domain names.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains the domain system as a distributed database with its own hierarchy of servers, and lays out a three-stage path for hosts to move over, with a timetable running from late 1986 to October 1989.
tldr.outcome: Hosts that could not convert were told where to get an equivalent of the host table once the central one was withdrawn. The document also lists the RFCs describing the system and the implementations available at the time.

facts.label: Policy announced
facts.value: October 1987, in a DDN Management Bulletin

today: RFC 1031 was published in November 1987 as an informational note for the DDN/MILNET community, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. Its timetable ended in October 1989, with the withdrawal of the central host table that the plan was built around.

sections.title: What This Document Is For
sections.content:
The RFC consolidates the information needed to implement domain style names throughout the DDN/MILNET Internet community. Although no official policy has been published, the introduction of domain style names will affect all hosts in the DDN/MILNET Internet, so the document is written as an aid to implementors and administrators.

It provides three things: an overview of the transition process from host tables to domains, a potential timetable for the transition, and references to documentation and software relating to the DDN/ARPANET domain system.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a briefing for the people who have to make the change: what is happening, when it has to happen, and where to find the specification and the code.

sections.title: Host Tables and the Domain System
sections.content:
All MILNET hosts are expected to have a way of translating the name of any other host into its Internet address. The current method of name resolution is to look the information up in a table of all hosts, which is cumbersome and relies on a central point of information. The Network Information Center maintains the table of hosts registered in the MILNET Internet and their addresses, and the size of that table and the frequency of updates had reached the limits of manageability. The central host table is fetched by a host on a timely basis from the NIC, processed locally to pare or reformat the table, and used in name resolution.

The domain system uses a distributed database and software to perform the same functions as the host table. In this system, host resolvers query domain servers for name resolution and may cache answers for performance. The domain servers each maintain a portion of the hierarchical database under separate administrative authority and control, and redundancy is obtained by transferring data between cooperating servers.

The domain system had been operating successfully on the ARPANET for over a year. One indication of that success was that the NIC's central host table was no longer a complete list: the ARPANET no longer depended primarily on the host table. The domain system was being implemented on the MILNET with DoD military standard protocols, and the first step of the change had already been taken as required by DDN Management Bulletin number 32 of 22 January 1987: all host names were converted from a simple, flat namespace to a structured name consistent with domains. In the second step, servers acting as the root of the database hierarchy were put in place, and in the next step hosts were to move away from host table usage.
sections.plainLanguage: The old way was one big list, kept in one place and copied to everybody. The new way is a hierarchy: each server holds the part of the naming tree it is responsible for, and a machine asks a server rather than reading a file. The ARPANET had been running this way for a year by the time this RFC was written.

sections.title: Three Stages of Conversion
sections.content:
Not all hosts will change from host table to domain server usage at one time, so three stages of conversion are envisaged. They roughly correspond to continuing to use the host table for all applications, using the domain system for only some applications, and using the domain system for all applications. The stages exist simultaneously as various hosts convert their application software according to available resources.

In the first stage, host table only, a host depends entirely on the host table for name resolution. The table is obtained from the NIC's central copy and the resolution is done by local table scanning. Most hosts are in this stage. Certain hosts may find it infeasible ever to convert, owing to older architectures, unchangeable software or other considerations, and at the end of the conversion period the NIC will stop maintaining an internet host table. To continue operations, hosts that do not convert will need to obtain an equivalent of the host table from some source: another host with which a bilateral agreement has been negotiated offline, a community-of-interest host acting as central repository for that community, or a locally-maintained table of host names and addresses. Transfer of the table from the source is a matter of local implementation and bilateral agreements.

In the second stage, domain system and host table, a host uses both. A likely scenario is that applications such as TELNET and FTP use the domain system while MAIL continues to use the host table for name resolution; an alternate scenario is that batch-style applications such as MAIL use the domain system and the interactive applications convert later. This stage is viewed as transitory, as hosts convert over to using the domain system exclusively, and it is highlighted as a separate stage to emphasize the need during the transition for both the host table and the domain system.

In the third and final stage, domain system only, a host has completed conversion and uses the domain system exclusively, including correct processing of the mailbox and mail exchanger resource records.
sections.plainLanguage: Hosts move over one application at a time. First everything still uses the old list; then some applications use the new system and others still use the list; eventually everything uses the new system. A machine that is too old to change will have to find its own copy of the list, because the central one is going away.

sections.title: The Timetable
sections.content:
The table of milestones for the MILNET transition from host table to domain system sets four events with their dates. The operational testing of the root server software ran from December 1986 to July 1987. The policy was announced in a DDN Management Bulletin in October 1987. Host conversion ran from October 1987 to October 1989. The host table was discontinued in October 1989.

The operational testing of the root server software has been completed, voluntary conversion can begin immediately, and mandatory conversion is required by October 1989. After that date, hosts that have not converted need to obtain the host table equivalent by private arrangement, as described in the migration path above.
sections.plainLanguage: The servers were tested over the second half of 1986 and the first half of 1987. The policy was announced in the autumn of 1987, and the two years after that were for hosts to convert. When the period ended in October 1989, the central list was withdrawn.

sections.title: The Documentation and the Implementations
sections.content:
The Name Domain system is described in several documents maintained and available from the NIC in both online and hardcopy form, in the Request For Comments format. The RFC gives a short synopsis of each. RFC 799 is an early description of the concepts of a name domain system, exploratory in nature, offering scenarios for name resolution and mail forwarding. RFC 819 is a think piece about hierarchical naming conventions for internetworking applications, aligned along administrative rather than topological boundaries and designed for interoperation among heterogeneous naming environments, and also discusses mail relaying, name service approaches and naming authorities. RFC 920 contains a policy statement on the requirements for establishing a new domain in the ARPA Internet and introduces the limited set of top level domains. RFC 921 contains a policy statement on the implementation schedule of the ARPA Internet domain system as of October 1984. RFC 952 specifies the format of the host and address table maintained by the NIC, and RFC 953 contains the official specification of the Hostname Server Protocol, a TCP-based protocol used by hosts to obtain all or a portion of that centralized table. RFC 974 describes how mail systems are expected to route messages using domain system information, in particular how mailers should interpret mail exchanger resource records. RFC 1032 gives the guidelines for a domain administrator establishing a new domain, and RFC 1033 gives procedures for domain administrators operating a domain server and maintaining their portion of the hierarchical database. RFC 1034 introduces domain style names and their use for mail and host address support, and discusses the hierarchical database model, resource record usage, query formation, query resolution and domain control. RFC 1035 specifies the format of domain system transactions and discusses the implementation of domain servers.

Several implementations of the domain system existed, and the intent of listing them was to give vendors the opportunity to inspect working code that embodies experience with the domain system. The two prominent and most mature were JEEVES, a TOPS-20 root server and resolver maintained by Paul Mockapetris, and BIND, the resolver and server for 4BSD systems maintained by Mike Karels, with a commercial version distributed with version 3.2 of the Sun Microsystems operating system. Others were in development: a port of BIND to MS-DOS by FTP Software, a TOPS-20 resolver by Rob Austein, a resolver for the Symbolics Lisp Machines, a Xerox Cedar resolver at Xerox PARC, a Harris resolver handling canonical name, host address, name server and mail agent records, a Fuzzball server and resolver, a Multics resolver, a partial VAX/VMS resolver in the CMU/TEK TCP/IP package, and a Macintosh port of BIND.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC points to eleven documents describing the system, from the early concepts through to the file format of the transactions between servers, and then lists the software that implemented it: a TOPS-20 program called JEEVES, and BIND, which was written for the 4BSD systems and also shipped with a commercial operating system. The point of the list was to let vendors read working code.

sections.title: Where to Get the Documents
sections.content:
The documents are available online from the NIC, at IP address 10.0.0.51 or 26.0.0.73, by using FTP with the login ANONYMOUS and the password GUEST. The RFCs are in files named RFC:RFCnnn.TXT and are simple ASCII files ready for printing, with pages separated by a form feed character on a line by itself.

Hardcopy of the documents and of the software mentioned in the discussions above may be obtained from the NIC or from the author. Prices are available on request and are documented in DDN Newsletter number 50 of 12 December 1986.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything was published in the ordinary way: fetch the files by anonymous FTP from the NIC, or order paper copies. The machine-readable copies were plain text with form feeds between pages, ready to print.
